title: What's permaculture all about?
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss permaculture: its definition as conscious design of agriculturally productive systems with the diversity, stability and resilience of natural ecosystems; origins in 1970s Australia with Bill Mollison and David Holmgren; three ethics (care for earth, care for people, setting limits on population and consumption); design principles such as zones and sectors, relative location, multiple functions, energy efficiency, biological resources, plant succession, nutrient recycling and diversity; a Schumacher College yield study comparing permaculture and conventional gardening plots; forest gardens; Josh's backyard permaculture redesign in Atlanta with a cistern and swale; and criticisms of permaculture as under-tested scientifically. The episode closes with a listener mail about unpaid fashion internships.

segments.title: Opening banter and live shows
segments.summary: Hosts riff on their New York City live shows and tease an upcoming Existential Risks episode featuring Charles C. Mann, whose book The Wizard and the Prophet is coming out. They introduce permaculture as a topic and Josh's urban permaculture yard project in Atlanta.

segments.title: What permaculture is and sustainability vs unsustainability
segments.summary: The hosts define permaculture as design principles for sustainable food production, contrasting it with big modern monoculture agriculture and explaining sustainable versus unsustainable farming, including fertilizer runoff and algae blooms. They use a river and dog-scratching analogy to describe managed interaction with land.

segments.title: Origins of permaculture and the Mollison-Holmgren split
segments.summary: Permaculture is traced to 1970s Australia, where Bill Mollison and David Holmgren coined the term from permanent and agriculture. The hosts describe the three ethics of care for earth, care for people, and setting limits on population and consumption, and note the two founders later split over different approaches.

segments.title: Permaculture definition and the three ethics explained
segments.summary: The hosts read a widely cited definition of permaculture about conscious design of productive systems with ecosystem diversity and stability, and discuss care for earth, care for people (including access to clean water), and limits on population and consumption. They also mention the book 1491 on ancient land management.

segments.title: Design principles: zones, sectors, relative location, multiple functions
segments.summary: The hosts walk through permaculture design principles including zones and sectors for placing elements by how much attention they need and by sun, wind, and water, relative location such as placing crops downhill from a pond, and single elements with multiple functions such as a pond serving irrigation, livestock water, and a barrier.

segments.title: Diversity, biological resources, succession, and nutrient cycling
segments.summary: The hosts cover further principles: diversifying so one loss does not wipe out a farm (using an egg-basket story), energy efficiency and windbreaks, using biological resources like ducks for snails, using pigs or chickens to till and rotate crops, native ladybugs versus store-bought ones carrying parasites, plant succession toward forest, and composting.

segments.title: Schumacher College yield study
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a three-year study by Bethan Stagg at Schumacher College comparing permaculture plots with conventional gardening plots. Conventional gardening yielded more food per area (13 versus 2.3 kilograms per hundred square meters), but permaculture required far less time and effort, and held up better in a year of bad weather.

segments.title: Forest gardens and Josh's Atlanta backyard redesign
segments.summary: The hosts describe the forest garden technique, a layered food garden imitating a natural forest with trees, shade-loving vines and plants. Josh describes his family's Atlanta backyard redesign by a permaculture designer, including a large cistern collecting roof water, a pump, and a swale with a small pond.

segments.title: Criticisms of permaculture and Mollison's views
segments.summary: The hosts note that permaculture is criticized for lacking rigorous scientific testing, and mention that Mollison reportedly advocated exotic plants, which conflicts with native-plant approaches. They also say Mollison was considered dogmatic.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact info
segments.summary: The hosts mention searching for permaculture on HowStuffWorks, invite listener contact by social media and email, and sign off.

segments.title: Listener mail on unpaid fashion internships
segments.summary: Listener Gail describes an unpaid fashion design internship in New York that required an all-black wardrobe and expensive housing, and argues that unpaid internships hurt diversity in the fashion industry.
